This rifle has seen too much. Worn finish, rounded edges, dust in every seam — and wrapped around the stock, a wide pink rubber band holding a small first aid kit in place. During the Soviet war in Afghanistan, soldiers didn't have room in their pockets or pouches for medical supplies, so they improvised. They used an Esmarch tourniquet, meant to stop catastrophic bleeding, as a giant rubber band to strap their first aid kit directly onto the rifle stock. On weapons like the AKS-74, the hollow folding stock even created a perfect pocket for it. It kept the kit within reach, protected from loss, and as a bonus, insulated the freezing metal in winter. It wasn't official. It wasn't pretty. But it worked. This is the kind of quiet battlefield ingenuity that never makes the history books.

title: Why soviet soldiers strapped their first aid kit to the rifle
